content: "The passage critiques the enduring 19th-century “great man” theory of history: the notion that exceptionally gifted and charismatic individuals singlehandedly drive major historical change through force of personality and genius. It notes that this idea has remained influential even after the emergence of egalitarian and Marxist approaches to history, including EP Thompson’s 1960s “history from below,” which emphasized ordinary people and social forces rather than elites. The Scottish philosopher Thomas Carlyle is presented as a key proponent of the hero-centered view, celebrating figures such as Aristotle, Julius Caesar, Napoleon, Martin Luther, and the prophet Muhammad as towering individuals whose actions decisively reshaped their worlds, while the majority of humanity supposedly could only observe and follow. Although the author calls this framework “daft,” they acknowledge its continuing appeal and persistence. The text then shifts to a modern political and moral warning: there remain people—predominantly men—who believe they are destined for heroic leadership, imagining a unique mission or sacred duty to act as national saviors. These self-styled heroes claim superior insight, insist they know best, and possess the ruthlessness and arrogance to impose their will on others. However, the passage argues that in the modern era such powerful figures rarely match the common understanding of “heroes.” Instead, they are more accurately described as anti-heroes or outright villains who still, like Carlyle’s chosen few, command substantial power."
